standalone.whatItIsAbout: It claims that every action or way of thinking that is individual, rather than shared, provokes fear.
standalone.insight: Individuality and departure from the common way are met with fear.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Under the morality of custom, any individual action or original thought provoked dread, so original spirits suffered by being felt, and feeling themselves, to be evil.
fidelity.reason: The excerpt drops the historical condition (under the dominion of the morality of custom), so it reads as a timeless universal claim rather than a description of a particular moral regime.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: A satirical remark that 'extending the Blessings of Civilization' to colonized peoples has really been a profitable trade that can still pay if worked carefully.
standalone.insight: The supposedly benevolent civilizing mission is exposed as a commercial enterprise run for profit.

fidelity.meaningInSource: In mock-businesslike satire, the author says the civilizing trade has paid well and still has money in it, but no longer enough to justify the risk, as the 'darkness' grows scarce.
fidelity.reason: The satirical reading survives; only the immediate 'but not enough' turn of the joke is lost.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It says the most important person is whoever you are with right now and the most important task is to do them good.
standalone.insight: Since we cannot know whom else we will meet, our duty and purpose lie in doing good to the person in front of us now.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Alongside the claim that now is the only important time, the most important person is the one present and the most important thing is to do them good.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the source; it only omits the parallel point about time.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It says that in magic and in life only the present moment exists.
standalone.insight: Only the present is real; past and future are not where life happens.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Only the present exists; time does not pass, though people struggle to focus on it, dwelling on past and future.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading is consistent with the passage.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: Some unnamed thing is described as not absolute truth about life and death but something that helps us live and face daily challenges.
standalone.insight: What matters is practical help for living rather than absolute truth.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The wisdom that matters is not absolute truth or book learning but the practical knowledge living in the hearts of people of good will that helps us live.
fidelity.reason: The reading does not distort the source, but it cannot identify the subject (heartfelt knowledge), so the meaning is vaguer.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: Writing advice to prefer short words over long ones whenever they work.
standalone.insight: Plain, short words are preferable to long ones when they serve equally well.

fidelity.meaningInSource: One of a list of writing rules: use a short word where one suffices, though any rule should be broken rather than write something barbarous.
fidelity.reason: Consistent with the source; only the closing caveat that the rules may be broken is lost.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It says love may lead us to suffering or bliss, but it always moves us somewhere.
standalone.insight: Love's defining trait is not whether it brings joy or pain but that it never leaves us where we were.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Love, always new, may bring hell or paradise but always takes us somewhere, and we must accept it as what nourishes our existence.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the passage.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It argues that a government unwilling to use violence to defend itself would quickly be overthrown by less scrupulous people.
standalone.insight: Political order depends on a willingness to use force, because scruples alone cannot survive against the unscrupulous.

fidelity.meaningInSource: As part of the argument that civilisation rests on coercion, a government refusing violence in self-defence would soon be overthrown.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading is consistent with the author's argument.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It defines when a society becomes totalitarian: when a ruling class that has lost its function holds on to power by force or fraud.
standalone.insight: Totalitarianism arises when power outlives its legitimate function and must be maintained artificially.

fidelity.meaningInSource: A society becomes totalitarian when its ruling class has lost its function but keeps power by force or fraud, which then makes it intolerant of truth and sincere writing.
fidelity.reason: The definition is stated as the author holds it.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It describes a nameless, unexplained love, unlike romantic, parental or divine love, that simply flows like a river.
unresolvedReferences: a love with no name (whose love, for whom, is never said)
standalone.insight: Some love exists outside every category and needs no reason, as a river needs no reason for its course.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The speaker describes the love they give the addressee as one with no name or explanation, outside the usual kinds of love, that asks nothing and simply exists.
fidelity.reason: Consistent with the source, though the personal declaration and the 'asks for nothing' quality are lost.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It says the true justification for democracy is that humans are too fallen to be trusted with unchecked power over others, the reverse of some unstated view.
standalone.insight: Democracy is justified not by human goodness but by human corruption: no one can be trusted with unchecked power.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Democracy is justified not because people are wise enough to govern but because mankind is so fallen that no one can be trusted with unchecked power.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reader gets the author's point even without the reversed premise.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It observes that telling people war is evil just gets a laugh, because everyone already knows it.
standalone.insight: Declaring an obvious moral truth is met with derision because it costs nothing to agree with it.

fidelity.meaningInSource: It is the setup for a contrast: everyone agrees war is evil, but when told patriotism is evil people exempt their own kind of patriotism.
fidelity.reason: Consistent with the source; the point about patriotism the line sets up is lost, but nothing is distorted.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It states the humanist view that a struggle must go on and that death is the cost of living.
standalone.insight: Mortality is the price we pay for life, and the humanist accepts this rather than seeking escape.

fidelity.meaningInSource: In contrast to the Christian wish to escape earthly struggle into heaven, the humanist holds that the painful struggle of earthly life must continue and death is its price.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading is consistent with the author's contrast, even though the Christian foil is omitted.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: A speaker asks what lasting benefit some unnamed thing brings 'us' unless it is used to bring souls to 'Our Father Below', apparently the devil.

fidelity.meaningInSource: A senior devil, voiced satirically by the author, says war's suffering is pleasant for devils but useless unless it is used to damn souls.
fidelity.reason: The excerpt is the view of a devil the author satirises; attributed to the author, it presents a view he rejects.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It argues that science and art as currently practised do not aid human progress but hinder it, like clumsy oar-splashing in a boat already drifting downstream.
standalone.insight: Activities that claim credit for progress may actually obstruct a movement that would happen anyway.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Science and art as currently practised hinder humanity's progress, as shown by their achievements being inaccessible to the labouring masses.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the author's claim.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It says the higher one's conception of God, the better one knows Him, and knowing Him draws one nearer to imitate His goodness and love.
standalone.insight: A deeper understanding of God leads to closeness to God and to imitating divine goodness.

fidelity.meaningInSource: A character arguing against sectarian pride says a higher conception of God brings truer knowledge of Him and leads people to imitate His goodness and love of man.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading is consistent with the speaker's point, which the narrative endorses.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It claims that no thinking person could live in a society like ours without wanting to change it.
standalone.insight: Our society is so flawed that any reflective person would want to reform it.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Any thinking person in present-day capitalist, imperialist Britain must want to change it, as the author has tried to do through his writing.
fidelity.reason: The specific target, capitalist society, is lost, but the general reading is not something the author would object to.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: The speaker recounts knowing of pacifist sects such as Mennonites, Herrnhuters and Quakers who forbid Christians from using weapons or serving in the military.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The author knew of the existence of pacifist sects but little of what they had written on non-resistance to evil.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading is consistent with what the author says.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It describes 'Gift-love' as wanting to give some woman happiness, comfort, protection and, if possible, wealth.
standalone.insight: Giving love seeks to provide for the beloved.

fidelity.meaningInSource: In a contrast of three kinds of love for a woman, Gift-love is the kind that wants to give her happiness, comfort, protection and wealth.
fidelity.reason: Consistent with the source, though the contrast with Need-love and Appreciative love is lost.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It claims that tyranny sincerely exercised for its victims' own good may be the most oppressive kind.
standalone.insight: Well-meaning oppression can be worse than selfish oppression, because sincere conviction knows no limit.

fidelity.meaningInSource: A tyranny exercised for the good of its victims may be the worst, since moral busybodies torment without end with their conscience's approval.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the author's view.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: The speaker grants Aristotle that some people may be fit only to be slaves, but rejects slavery because no one is fit to be a master.
standalone.insight: The case against slavery rests not on everyone's fitness for freedom but on no one's fitness to rule others.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The author accepts Aristotle's claim but rejects slavery because no man is fit to be a master, in line with his view that no one can be trusted with unchecked power.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the source.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It argues that so-called great men in history are merely labels naming events and have little real connection to them.
standalone.insight: History is not driven by great individuals; they merely lend their names to events.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Great men are only labels for historical events; their seemingly free actions are bound by the whole course of history.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading is consistent with the passage.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It says British press freedom was always partly fake because money controls opinion, but that legal free speech still leaves loopholes for unorthodox writers.
standalone.insight: Formal free speech is compromised by money, yet still matters because the legal right leaves space for dissent.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Press freedom in Britain was partly a fake due to money's control of opinion, but legal free speech left loopholes, a state of affairs the author fears will end.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading is consistent with the author's view.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It says that the only alternative to risking the tragedy of love is damnation, since only Hell is safe from love's dangers.
standalone.insight: Avoiding love's risks to stay safe is itself a kind of damnation.

fidelity.meaningInSource: To refuse love in order to stay safe is to lock the heart away until it becomes irredeemable; the alternative to risking love's tragedy is damnation.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the author's point.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It affirms that the ancient saying 'the partial becomes complete' is true and that all real completion falls under it.
standalone.insight: True wholeness comes from what is partial or incomplete.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Concluding a passage on humility and non-striving, it affirms that the saying 'the partial becomes complete' is true and encompasses all real completion.
fidelity.reason: Consistent with the source, though the link to humility and yielding that gives the saying its meaning is lost.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: The speaker, raised in some tradition, says he sympathises with it because even at its worst it is better than the shallow self-righteousness of left-wing intellectuals.
standalone.insight: Even a stupid, sentimental tradition can be more admirable than self-righteous enlightened contempt for it.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The author, raised in the tradition of patriotic loyalty, sympathises with it because even at its worst it is better than the left-wing intelligentsia's sneering self-righteousness.
fidelity.reason: The reading is consistent but cannot identify the tradition as patriotism, so the point is vaguer.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It argues that the levelling attitude of 'I'm as good as you' should be resisted in personal and spiritual life as firmly as bureaucracy or privilege are resisted in politics.
standalone.insight: Equality is right as a political principle but corrosive when it becomes an inner attitude that refuses to recognise anything higher than oneself.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The author holds that political equality must be paired with an inner acceptance of hierarchy, so the egalitarian spirit should be kept out of personal and spiritual life.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the author's position; the rest of the passage only elaborates it.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It says that a decent world is indivisible: either everyone shares in it or no one really has it.
standalone.insight: Human welfare is interdependent; decency cannot be secured for some while denied to others.

fidelity.meaningInSource: In arguing that Indian independence and British workers' interests align against capitalist exploitation and fascism, the author states that a decent world must be shared by all or by none.
fidelity.reason: The general claim of shared fate is exactly what the author asserts; the source just applies it to India and Britain.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It asserts that art ought never to aim at popularity.
standalone.insight: Art loses its integrity when it tries to please the public.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Because the public demands that art flatter and amuse it, the author insists art must never try to be popular; the public should instead become artistic.
fidelity.reason: The excerpt states the author's own conclusion without distortion.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It observes that spending the night outdoors in London is miserable, particularly for a poor, ragged, hungry person.

fidelity.meaningInSource: It opens a description of homeless people's plight in London that leads to a criticism of Parliament and England's apparent prosperity.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading is consistent; the excerpt merely omits the later social criticism.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It quotes Oedipus saying all is well and declares that this acceptance is sacred.
standalone.insight: Affirming one's fate, even after catastrophe, has a kind of sacred dignity.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Oedipus's affirmation is sacred because it shows that not everything is exhausted and makes fate a human matter rather than a god's imposition of futile suffering.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading of a sacred acceptance is consistent, though it misses the source's point that the remark humanises fate and drives out the god.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It describes some unspecified people progressing from devoted followers to evangelists and finally to fanatics.
standalone.insight: Devotion can escalate step by step into fanaticism.

fidelity.meaningInSource: People who turn to religion to give life meaning and believe they are doing God's work escalate from devout followers to evangelists to fanatics.
fidelity.reason: The escalation reading is consistent, but the standalone reader cannot know it concerns religious believers seeking meaning.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It notes that a navy employs relatively few people and, being directed outward, cannot directly influence domestic politics.

fidelity.meaningInSource: It explains why there are military dictatorships but no naval ones, as part of an account of English dislike of militarism.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading accurately reflects the claim; the conclusion drawn from it is simply omitted.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It asserts that nobility comes only from birth and blood, not from anything acquired.
standalone.insight: Nobility is inherited, not earned.

fidelity.meaningInSource: It opens a racialist argument that spiritual nobility is a pretence, with an antisemitic aside, and that only blood ennobles.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the stated claim, but it loses the racial and antisemitic framing that gives 'blood' its meaning in the source.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It says truth is one route toward the good but is in itself neither the good nor the beautiful.
standalone.insight: Truth is instrumental rather than intrinsically good or beautiful.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Truth serves the good only as one approach and is not itself good or beautiful, since by exposing deception it destroys the illusion on which beauty depends.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading is consistent with the passage; the explanation about illusion is just omitted.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It claims that without money, people will not care for or love you in the final, decisive measure.
standalone.insight: Love and regard may survive poverty in part, but the last, essential degree of them depends on money.

fidelity.meaningInSource: In a bitter rant that all human relationships are bought with money, the speaker says that without money people withhold the last bit of care and love that matters.
fidelity.reason: The cynical standalone reading matches the speaker's view, though it loses the bitter, self-pitying tone of the surrounding rant.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It suggests that civilisation has made us too sophisticated to see plain truths.
standalone.insight: Refinement can blind us to simple truths.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Civilised people fail to grasp the simple truth that survival often requires fighting and that war, though evil, is often the lesser evil.
fidelity.reason: The general reading is consistent, though the specific 'obvious' truth (the necessity of war) is lost.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: The speaker says two selves, the Animal and the Diabolical, compete within him against the human self he must try to become.
standalone.insight: Becoming fully human means overcoming both animal appetite and a worse, spiritual malice within.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Explaining why spiritual sins are worse than fleshly ones, the speaker names the Animal and Diabolical selves competing with the human self, and holds that the Diabolical is worse.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading is consistent; it only misses the point that the Diabolical self is the worse of the two.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It points out that rulers call themselves by the very lowly names, such as orphans or men of little virtue, that ordinary people most dislike.
standalone.insight: Those with the most power deliberately adopt humble self-descriptions; greatness is expressed through self-abasement.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Rulers adopt self-deprecating titles that others dislike, illustrating that some things are increased by being diminished.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading of a paradox of humility in power matches the source's point.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It defends some unspecified dream as good and harmless despite being historically unrealistic.
standalone.insight: A belief can be naive about history and still worth respecting if it is good and not exploitative.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The author defends a messianic dream of brotherhood as deserving sympathy, since it is well-meant and not a fraud, even if historically unrealistic.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading is consistent in attitude, but the reader cannot know what dream is meant.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It claims that what the public dislikes above all is novelty.
standalone.insight: People resist the new more than anything else.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The public dislike novelty in art, such as extensions of its subject matter, because they fear the artist's individualism.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading is consistent but generalises a claim the source makes specifically about art.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: The speaker rejects some unstated belief and concludes that someone must have sent us here for a purpose.
standalone.insight: Our existence implies a purpose given by someone else.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Nekhludoff rejects the belief that we are lords of the world made for our enjoyment and concludes that we were sent here by a Master for a purpose.
fidelity.reason: The conclusion about purpose is consistent, but the reader cannot know which belief is rejected.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: A man facing a particular death realises that fearing it means fearing life.
unresolvedReferences: this death he was staring at
standalone.insight: Fear of death is really fear of life.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The character realises that terror of death amounts to fear of life, since those who fear death are those who never fully lived.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the passage's meaning.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It says certain miracles retell in small form the same story written across the whole world in letters too large for some to see.
standalone.insight: Small, local wonders make visible a larger pattern that is too vast to notice.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Miracles do locally and visibly what God does universally, acting either as reminders of what He has done or prophecies of what He will do.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading is consistent with the source's meaning.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It says some motto deserved removal for the unanswerable reason that it stated a lie.
standalone.insight: The best reason to remove a statement is that it is false.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The motto 'In God We Trust' should have been removed from coinage because the nation no longer trusts in God but in the dollar.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading is consistent; the reader just does not know which motto or why it is a lie.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: The speaker insists that he had been, still was, and always was right.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Facing execution, the narrator feels vindicated in the life he lived, since in an absurd universe nothing matters and all are condemned by the same fate.
fidelity.reason: Alone it reads as stubborn self-righteousness, while in the source it is an existential vindication in the face of death and absurdity.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It says the wise person has no fixed mind of his own but adopts the mind of the people.
standalone.insight: Wisdom, especially in leadership, means setting aside a rigid self and taking on the concerns of others.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The sage lacks a fixed mind of his own and identifies with the people, treating all with goodness and sincerity as his children.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the source.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It tells the reader not to rely on positive-thinking affirmations because they already know they are loved, strong and capable.
standalone.insight: Genuine self-worth does not need repeated affirmation; affirmations imply doubt.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Since you are what you believe yourself to be, you need no positive-thinking affirmations; you already know your worth, and when you doubt it you should laugh.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading is consistent with the source's advice.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It says totalitarianism destroys a certain shared basis of agreement that implies all humans are one species.
standalone.insight: Totalitarianism attacks the shared ground of fact that underlies our common humanity.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Totalitarianism destroys the body of neutral, objective fact that even opposing historians accept, and with it the idea of a common humanity.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading is consistent, though it lacks the specific point about objective fact.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: Someone tells a specific addressee that they had a long, proud reputation for honesty which they treasured above all.

fidelity.meaningInSource: A vengeful stranger explains that the townspeople's proud reputation for honesty was the vanity he targeted, since untested virtue is the weakest of all.
fidelity.reason: Alone it can read as plain acknowledgement or praise, while in the source it is contemptuous, identifying the pride as a weakness to exploit.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: The speaker recounts landing by chance in a Western European community where political awareness and rejection of capitalism were the norm.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The author describes how the workers' militias concentrated revolutionary sentiment, so he found himself in a community where anti-capitalist political consciousness was normal.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the source.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It claims that nothing is useless in God's eyes, so nothing, not a leaf, hair or insect, perishes for lack of purpose.
standalone.insight: Everything in creation has meaning and purpose before God.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Everything has a reason to exist in God's eyes, so one need not strive to be useful but simply to be oneself.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading is consistent with the source.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: Anyone who earnestly and persistently desires joy will eventually find it.
standalone.insight: Sincere, sustained desire for joy is itself what secures it; missing joy implies not truly wanting it.

fidelity.meaningInSource: In a dialogue about heaven and hell, it asserts that every soul which truly and steadily wants (heavenly) joy reaches it, since those in hell have chosen it.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the claim; only the theological framing of joy as salvation and hell as self-chosen is lost.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: Some unnamed thing whose only aesthetic flaw, to readers shaped by romanticism, is being slightly too orderly.
standalone.insight: A sensibility formed by romanticism can find perfect order itself an aesthetic fault.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The medieval model of the cosmos, sublimely ordered, may seem a little too ordered to modern readers shaped by romanticism.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading is consistent; it simply cannot identify the medieval cosmos as the subject.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: A convalescent writer joking that their handwriting and face have not yet recovered but they are otherwise regaining strength.

fidelity.meaningInSource: In a letter after an illness, the writer reassures her nephew that she is recovering well despite shaky handwriting and appearance.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading of a personal health update matches the source.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: A claim that Italians are self-assured because they are excitable and easily forget themselves and others.
standalone.insight: Self-assurance can stem from excitability and self-forgetfulness rather than reflection (offered as a national stereotype).

fidelity.meaningInSource: One item in a satirical catalogue of the different grounds of national self-assurance, building toward the claim that German self-assurance is the worst.
fidelity.reason: The claim itself is preserved; the comparative, satirical context of the list is lost.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: A writing rule: avoid figures of speech that are already familiar from print.
standalone.insight: Familiar metaphors are dead language; good writing requires fresh imagery rather than stock phrases.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The first of several writing rules: do not use stale, familiar figures of speech.
fidelity.reason: The rule is stated as the author means it; the later escape clause about barbarous prose does not change it.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: The observation that nobody seems ever to write approvingly about an execution.
standalone.insight: Even those who accept executions never celebrate them in writing, hinting at a shared moral unease.

fidelity.meaningInSource: It opens the argument that capital punishment is accepted as necessary yet instinctively felt to be wrong, which is why accounts of executions are written with horror.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading is consistent with the author's observation.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: Someone skilled at managing the life entrusted to them moves untouched among wild beasts and armed soldiers.
standalone.insight: Rightly ordering one's life makes one invulnerable to external dangers.

fidelity.meaningInSource: In contrast to those who court death by striving too hard to preserve life, the one who handles life rightly (without clinging) has no place in him for death to enter.
fidelity.reason: The invulnerability claim is preserved; the contrast with excessive self-preservation, which defines what 'skilful' means, is lost.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: Temptation succeeds by exploiting genuine needs we have neglected in our values.
standalone.insight: Temptation is not purely alien; it feeds real hungers we have starved, so its pull reveals flaws in our own values.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Appeals to inequality (from romantic films to Nazi ideology) succeed because a culture of flat equality starves a real human need.
fidelity.reason: The general principle is exactly what the author asserts, applied in the source to a specific case.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: A man recalling his former truthfulness and realizing he now lives in a falsehood that everyone around him accepts as truth.
standalone.insight: A person can drift from integrity into a socially accepted falsehood that no one around them recognizes as false.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The character contrasts his former free, truthful self with his present entrapment in a false life that his surroundings accept as true.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the passage.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: The public ought to cultivate its own artistic sensibility.
standalone.insight: The burden of taste lies with the audience to rise to art, not merely to consume it.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Art should never stoop to popularity; instead the public should raise itself to art.
fidelity.reason: Consistent, but the pointed reversal against art pandering to the public is lost.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: A sardonic hope that in the next great war a warmonger might actually be wounded.
standalone.insight: Those who loudly cheer for war are never the ones who suffer in it.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Since jingoists never reach the front, the author takes grim comfort that air war might finally expose them to danger.
fidelity.reason: The sardonic reading matches the source's point.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: Swearing, especially English swearing, is mysterious and irrational, a kind of magic.
standalone.insight: Swearing works like magic: words gain power irrationally rather than through their meaning.

fidelity.meaningInSource: It introduces the author's discussion of the paradox that swear words lose the meaning that made them oaths.
fidelity.reason: The claim is the author's own; omitting the paradox is mere omission.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: A qualified concession that the distinction between atrocities and acts of war holds up to a point.
standalone.insight: The line between atrocity and legitimate war is real but limited.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The author grants the distinction is valid within the logic of accepting war, before suggesting that this whole moral framework is insane.
fidelity.reason: The qualifier 'so far as it goes' is kept, but the author's subsequent doubt about the whole framework is lost.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: All experiences are equivalent in some unspecified respect.

fidelity.meaningInSource: With respect to consciousness, which is what makes a clerk equal to a conqueror, no kind of experience is privileged over another.
fidelity.reason: Without the regard specified, the standalone reading can imply experiences simply do not matter, whereas the author says they matter through consciousness.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: A definition of atrocity as terrorism without genuine military purpose.
standalone.insight: What makes violence an atrocity is the absence of military purpose.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The author's working definition of atrocity, which he accepts within the logic of war before questioning that logic's sanity.
fidelity.reason: The definition is the author's, though his ironic distance from the framework is lost.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: Well-meaning people in an unjust system do the most harm, just as kind slave-owners hid slavery's horror.
standalone.insight: Kindness within an unjust system can perpetuate it by masking its cruelty, so those who try hardest to do good may do the most harm.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Philanthropic palliatives in England, like kind slave-owning, conceal and prolong the underlying injustice.
fidelity.reason: The excerpt is the whole source passage.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: Statements that are precisely true tend to look like paradoxes.
standalone.insight: Deep truth often appears contradictory to ordinary understanding.

fidelity.meaningInSource: It sums up the preceding truths (water's softness overcoming the hard, the one who bears reproach becoming king) as true words that seem paradoxical.
fidelity.reason: The general claim is consistent with how the author uses it.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: Turning to God only as a last resort, when one's life is no longer worth keeping, is a poor offering, and the writer calls something about this divine humility.
standalone.insight: Surrendering to God only when everything is lost is a meagre offering.

fidelity.meaningInSource: God's humility lies in accepting us even when we come to Him only as a last resort, which is a poor thing to offer.
fidelity.reason: The poorness of last-resort surrender is preserved; that the humility is God's, in accepting it, is unclear standalone.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: Every atom and mineral flake of some particular stone and mountain is a world in itself.
standalone.insight: Even the smallest fragment of matter can contain a whole world.

fidelity.meaningInSource: For Sisyphus, the rock and mountain of his fate become a full world of his own, part of seeing a masterless universe as neither sterile nor futile.
fidelity.reason: Not contradicted, but the standalone reading shifts it to a general claim about matter, losing the existential point about Sisyphus owning his fate.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: Spiritual needs, like bodily hunger, must be satisfied, and if denied proper nourishment they will seek harmful substitutes.
standalone.insight: Suppressed spiritual needs do not vanish; they attach themselves to poisonous substitutes.

fidelity.meaningInSource: When people are denied a legitimate object of reverence such as a monarch, their craving for inequality turns to worshipping millionaires, celebrities or gangsters.
fidelity.reason: The general principle is the author's own; the source applies it to monarchy.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: Uprooting the passions entirely amounts to attacking life itself, and the church's approach is therefore hostile to life.
standalone.insight: Eradicating the passions rather than refining them is an assault on life itself.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The church fights passions by excision rather than spiritualizing them, and this extirpation is hostile to life.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the author's claim.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: People today regard the laborer's position as a natural economic condition and do not recognize it as slavery, just as in some earlier case.
standalone.insight: Wage labor may be a form of slavery that goes unrecognized because it seems natural and inevitable.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Just as 18th-century Europeans failed to see serfdom as slavery, people now fail to see wage labor as slavery.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading captures the author's claim; only the serfdom comparison is unclear.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: The speaker has not spent their time picturing their home, desk, or side of the bed.

fidelity.meaningInSource: One reason the speaker does not feel like a foreigner: they have not been homesick or longing for home while traveling.
fidelity.reason: Consistent; the 'not a foreigner' framing is merely omitted.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: A parody of the biblical hymn to love that attributes all of love's virtues to money.
standalone.insight: Satirically, money has taken the place of love as society's supreme virtue.

fidelity.meaningInSource: A satirical rewriting of 1 Corinthians 13 that substitutes money for love, mocking the worship of money.
fidelity.reason: The parody is recognizable standalone, though the closing punchline that money is the greatest is omitted.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: Blaming one's afflictions on others or on oneself amounts to the same thing.
standalone.insight: Blaming others and blaming oneself for suffering are at bottom equivalent responses.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Both blaming others and blaming oneself are equally despicable forms of bewailing one's lot, since both insist someone must be to blame for suffering.
fidelity.reason: The equivalence is preserved, but the respect in which they are the same (equally weak and vengeful) is lost.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It states that in the nineteenth century, although parts of the world were unexplored, travel was almost unrestricted.

fidelity.meaningInSource: It opens the author's point that travel before 1914 was largely free of passports and border controls.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the historical observation the passage makes.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: Something unnamed finishes its work without claiming credit for having done it.
standalone.insight: Accomplishing something without seeking credit for it.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The Great Tao produces and sustains all things but does not claim credit or lordship over them.
fidelity.reason: The reader understands the idea of uncredited work; only the identity of the subject (the Tao) is lost, which does not distort the meaning.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: The speaker says that some departure now feels not like leaving but like returning.
standalone.insight: A departure into the unknown can feel like a homecoming.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The speaker's journey toward the longed-for Mountain feels like going home to the place she always belonged.
fidelity.reason: The standalone sense of a departure feeling like a return is consistent, though the longing for home that gives it weight is lost.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It describes raw material being cut up and shaped into vessels.

fidelity.meaningInSource: A metaphor: the simple, undivided original state, when divided, becomes useful instruments, as the sage becomes head of officials and governs without violence.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reader takes it as a literal remark about craftsmanship, losing the metaphorical point about the primal simplicity and governance that gives it meaning in the source.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It tells the reader they live within the Universe, which holds every solution and every problem.
standalone.insight: Everything we struggle with and everything that could resolve it already exists within the whole we belong to.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Within a passage about freeing oneself from memory, it says the Universe one inhabits contains all solutions and problems.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading is consistent with the passage.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It says that noticing small things is the key to clear sight and protecting what is soft is the key to strength.
standalone.insight: True clarity lies in attention to the small, and true strength in protecting the gentle rather than in force.

fidelity.meaningInSource: In the Taoist passage, perceiving the small and guarding the soft are the secrets of clear sight and strength.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the source's claim.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: The speaker says they cannot and will not fully give up the worldview formed in childhood.
standalone.insight: The worldview formed in childhood persists, and one may not even wish to shed it entirely.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The author explains that he keeps childhood sensibilities (love of prose style, nature, solid objects) even in political writing.
fidelity.reason: Consistent, though 'world view' in the source refers mainly to aesthetic likes and dislikes rather than beliefs in general.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: The speaker concedes that everyone, including themselves, accepts that the mind strongly influences the body.
standalone.insight: The mind has a powerful effect on the body.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The author affirms the mind's influence over the body, leading into examples of healers and placebo cures that exploit imagination.
fidelity.reason: The supplied passage affirms the claim, consistent with the standalone reading.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It claims that the word 'Fascism', as people use it, has become nearly meaningless.
standalone.insight: A political term used loosely enough loses its meaning.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The word 'Fascism' is applied to so many unrelated things that it has become almost meaningless.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the passage.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: Some flaw is attributed to our languages, social meanings, morals, philosophies and religions, which impose limits that do not really exist.
standalone.insight: Our frameworks of description and belief impose limits that reality itself does not have.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The apparent paradox of prescience and predestination arises from our descriptive and cultural frameworks, which impose limits where none exist.
fidelity.reason: The reader grasps the core claim about frameworks imposing false limits; only the specific flaw (the paradox of prescience) is lost.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It says that love is an act of faith rather than a transaction.
standalone.insight: Love is given in trust, not as a trade for something in return.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Loving while expecting love in return misses the point; love is given in faith, not exchanged.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the source.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: The speaker concedes, as if continuing an argument, that war is entertaining.
standalone.insight: War, for all its horror, has an entertaining side for those who watch it.

fidelity.meaningInSource: A devil remarks that war's human suffering is a pleasing refreshment for demons, but useless unless it wins souls for hell.
fidelity.reason: The speaker is a demon in a satirical voice; out of context the line reads as a human claim the author does not hold.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It says God is not the same as love, but that the more love there is, the more a person manifests God and truly exists.
standalone.insight: Love is not God itself but the means by which humans express the divine and become more fully real.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Love unites man's life with other lives, increasing his manifestation of God and so his true existence.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the passage.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: Rivers and seas receive all the streams because they lie lower than them, and that is what makes them their kings.
standalone.insight: Supremacy comes from placing oneself lower; humility is what draws others to you.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The rivers' lowliness is an image for how the sage ruler leads by placing himself below others.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading is consistent; the source only extends it to the sage.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It says we learn in the past but are not its product, and past feelings are of no use to the present.
standalone.insight: The past teaches us but does not define us, and its emotions cannot serve the present.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The present must be met on its own terms; the past neither explains nor helps what happens now.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the passage.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It claims that conquered, oppressed Hungary did more for freedom and justice than any nation in twenty years.
standalone.insight: A defeated people's resistance can serve freedom more than any victor's achievements.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Hungary's crushed uprising taught the world about freedom through its sacrifice, which the West must not betray.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading is consistent with the passage.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It laments how many people believe they cannot learn or that learning is hard.
standalone.insight: A widespread belief in one's inability to learn, or in learning's difficulty, is itself a barrier.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Contrasting with Muad'Dib's basic trust that he could learn, many people wrongly believe they cannot learn or that it is difficult.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the passage.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It says that striving upward is in itself enough to fulfil a person.
standalone.insight: Fulfilment lies in the struggle itself, not in reaching the goal.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Sisyphus' endless effort toward the summit is enough to fill his heart, so one must imagine him happy.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the passage.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It says that freeing yourself from memory is hard but reveals that you are capable of more than you thought.
standalone.insight: Letting go of the past, though difficult, uncovers unsuspected capacity.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Freeing oneself from memory is difficult but reveals one's greater capability, introducing the advice to visit one's soul rather than one's past.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the passage.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It says that whatever direction the priest takes, the teacher must take the opposite one.
standalone.insight: Education must stand in opposition to the clergy.

fidelity.meaningInSource: One of a string of satirical aphorisms, saying the teacher is bound to oppose the priest.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading is consistent; the satirical, notebook-aphorism tone is lost, but nothing is reversed.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: The writer mock-complains that Walter Scott, already famous as a poet, unfairly also writes good novels.

fidelity.meaningInSource: A tongue-in-cheek complaint of rivalry with Scott, ending with the admission that she will probably like Waverley.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading captures the playful complaint as in the source.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It says it is good to remember how insignificant one is among billions of people and animals, on a tiny earth, over vast ages.
standalone.insight: Remembering one's cosmic smallness is salutary.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Remembering one's insignificance is good, and leads to the view that one's only significance is to do one's assigned work.
fidelity.reason: Consistent with the author; it drops the counterbalancing idea that one has significance as a worker.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: The writer suggests the English should begin retreating from Delhi during the 1857 rebellion once the rainy season sets in.

fidelity.meaningInSource: A prediction he put forward as a newspaper's military correspondent, conditional on reports being true and admittedly worded to be right either way.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading presents a sincere recommendation, dropping the condition and the author's admission that it was a hedged, self-protective proposition.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: A verbless phrase naming the uprooting of sensuality, pride, love of power, love of property and revenge, apparently as an aim.

fidelity.meaningInSource: It names the passions the church tries to cut out, a method the author condemns as hostile to life.
fidelity.reason: Alone it can read as an endorsed ideal, while the author is describing and attacking the church's practice.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It says English working-class soldiers in the First World War met many foreigners but came back hating all Europeans except the Germans, whose courage they admired.
standalone.insight: Contact with foreigners does not necessarily breed understanding; it may harden prejudice.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Wartime contact with Europe left the English working class as insular as before, even hostile.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the passage.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: It says the new rich of the nineteenth century were strikingly irresponsible, seeing everything as individual success and barely aware of the community.
standalone.insight: A newly wealthy class without a tradition of public service sees only individual success and ignores the community.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The newly rich class Dickens belonged to lacked any tradition of public service, so it saw only individual success.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the passage.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: An aside brushing off the fact that humanity has repeatedly killed the very people it hailed as saviors.
standalone.insight: Humanity habitually destroys its own would-be saviors.

fidelity.meaningInSource: A concession, waved aside, that the hopeful dream of brotherhood runs against history's record of killing messiahs; the author still urges sympathy for the dream.
fidelity.reason: The author does hold that we slaughter our messiahs; the excerpt only loses that it is a dismissed concession in an argument for sympathy.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: A writing rule telling the reader to remove every word that can be removed.
standalone.insight: Concision: prose improves when every unnecessary word is cut.

fidelity.meaningInSource: One of a list of writing rules, all of which the author says should be broken sooner than writing something barbarous.
fidelity.reason: Consistent with the author; only the closing caveat that the rules are not absolute is lost.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: An exhortation to venture boldly into the unknown.
standalone.insight: One should take risks and explore the unknown rather than stay safe.

fidelity.meaningInSource: One of a series of exhortations to 'live dangerously' addressed to seekers of knowledge, as the secret to the most fruitful existence.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading of bold risk-taking matches; the source's more aggressive conquering framing is lost but not contradicted.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: The moment the public realized that writing could be as powerful and aggressive a weapon as street violence, presented as a calamity.
standalone.insight: Discovering that words can be wielded as weapons was a fateful, regrettable turn; the pen can be as brutal as a thrown brick.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The public's discovery that the pen could serve as a weapon led to the rise of journalism as a force of prejudice and twaddle, which the author regrets.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches; the specific target, journalism, is lost but nothing is distorted.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: Some unidentified man for whom the greatest happiness is satisfying his desires as fully as possible.

fidelity.meaningInSource: A description of the 'savage' conception of life, which the author presents as self-centred and primitive, not as his own view of happiness.
fidelity.reason: The reader sees it as describing someone, which is consistent, but shown alone it can easily read as the author's own endorsed definition of happiness, which the source critiques.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: Our absurd and tragic habit of demanding certain qualities while destroying the conditions that make them possible.
standalone.insight: Societies loudly demand virtues while undermining the very things that produce them.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Modern education and culture remove the moral formation that produces drive, self-sacrifice and virtue, while still demanding those qualities.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading of demanding what we make impossible is exactly the author's point; only the specifics are omitted.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: A rhetorical question asking whether some deep longing was ultimately meaningless.
standalone.insight: Deep longing may carry a meaning of its own rather than being in vain.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The speaker suggests that a lifelong longing for a beautiful, home-like place was meaningful, because reaching it now feels like going back home.
fidelity.reason: The question implies the longing meant something, as the source does; the object of the longing and the sense of homecoming are lost.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: A description of a group of employees as tough, Americanized go-getters who hold nothing sacred but money.

fidelity.meaningInSource: A description of the advertising firm's staff as money-worshipping cynics, later shown to be naive believers in the money-god.
fidelity.reason: The description is the same in and out of context.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: A question suggesting that fifty remaining years of life is not fundamentally different from half an hour.
standalone.insight: However long we have left, our time is finite and brief, so we should live as though death were near.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Since a person who knew he would die in half an hour would avoid trivial or bad acts, one with fifty years should live the same way, because the difference is insignificant.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading of life's brevity matches; the explicit moral consequence about avoiding trivial and bad deeds is lost.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: A hopeful anticipation of the day humanity's true personality will be revealed.
standalone.insight: Humanity's true nature has not yet been realized, and its eventual emergence will be wonderful.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The opening of a vision of the future true personality of man, which will grow naturally, be wise without striving, and help others by being what it is.
fidelity.reason: The hopeful anticipation is exactly what the author expresses; the details are simply omitted.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: A scornful claim that virtually everything humans say or write is plagiarism.
standalone.insight: Nearly all human expression is borrowed from others; originality is largely an illusion.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Mocking a plagiarism accusation, the author argues that substantially all ideas are second-hand and the true material of human utterance is borrowed.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading is the author's sincere view; only the occasion of the remark is lost.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: Pleasure as the signal by which nature shows approval of what we do.
standalone.insight: Pleasure is a natural indicator that we are living rightly.

fidelity.meaningInSource: When man lives fully and his activities are pleasurable, that pleasure is nature's sign that he is in harmony with himself, though what he seeks is life, not pleasure itself.
fidelity.reason: Consistent with the author; the nuance that pleasure is a sign rather than the goal is somewhat lost, inviting a more hedonistic reading.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: A writing rule to prefer the active voice over the passive.

fidelity.meaningInSource: One of a list of writing rules that the author says should be broken sooner than writing something barbarous.
fidelity.reason: The rule is stated as the author states it; the caveat that the rules are not absolute is lost.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: A fragment saying some people dislike working long hours underground, in water or heat, or at night in factories making things for 'our' pleasure.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Part of an argument that we cannot pretend not to know that workers hate the gruelling labour that produces our comforts, and that our police and soldiers exist to keep them at it.
fidelity.reason: The workers' suffering for our pleasure is consistent with the author; the point that we cannot deny knowing it is lost.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: The claim that landowners originally took their land by force and only later had it legitimized through legal documents.
standalone.insight: Ownership of land rests on past violence that the law afterwards dressed up as legitimate title.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Land ownership, as with the English enclosures, originated in seizure by force, later legitimized by lawyers.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the author's claim exactly.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: An interview exchange in which Tolkien corrects the idea that Middle-earth is our world in another era, saying it is our world at a different stage of imagination.
standalone.insight: Middle-earth is not a distant past of our world but our world as imagined differently.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Tolkien, having explained Middle-earth is an old word for this world, corrects the interviewer: it differs not in era but in stage of imagination.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the exchange.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: A remark that behind some visible game of deadlocks and bottle-necks, a more serious game is being played.
unresolvedReferences: the game of deadlocks and bottle-necks

fidelity.meaningInSource: An introduction: behind diplomatic manoeuvring lies a more serious game governed by axioms about surrendering sovereignty.
fidelity.reason: The reading of a more serious game behind the surface one is consistent; it just lacks what that game is.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: The idea that good and evil are steadily diverging, leaving less and less room for neutrality.
standalone.insight: Over time moral differences sharpen and polarize, and the middle ground of neutrality disappears.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Everything in the universe hardens and narrows over time, so contrasts grow sharper and choices more momentous, leaving less room for neutrality.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading is what the passage says.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: The claim that people love because they have an inner need to love.
standalone.insight: Love springs from an inner need, not from any reason or reward.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Love is an act of faith, not an exchange; we love out of our own need, not expecting to be loved in return.
fidelity.reason: Consistent with the source; the explicit contrast with love as an exchange is lost.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: Advice to avoid risk and simply imitate whatever is already successful.
standalone.insight: Safety lies in imitating proven success rather than taking risks.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The mindset of fearful, ass-covering corporate bureaucrats, which the author describes critically.
fidelity.reason: Shown alone it reads as the author's advice, but in the source it voices the code of people the author criticizes.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: English people's deep dislike of swaggering military officers and military display.
standalone.insight: The English across classes instinctively loathe militaristic swagger.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The English hate the swaggering army officer type, which helps explain why militarism, unlike naval power, is distrusted at home.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the author's claim.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: Some unspecified facts that are felt intuitively but need careful study before the mind can grasp them.
standalone.insight: Some truths are felt by the heart before the intellect can understand them.

fidelity.meaningInSource: The urgency of the question of whether life is worth living is something the heart feels but which needs study before the intellect grasps it.
fidelity.reason: The general heart-before-intellect reading is consistent; the specific facts about suicide and life's worth are lost.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: The opposition between sincere speech and elegant, embellished speech.
standalone.insight: Truthful words tend to be plain, and polished words tend to be insincere.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Sincere words are plain and fine words insincere, opening a series of paradoxes about true wisdom.
fidelity.reason: Identical meaning in and out of context.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: Ordinary believers should not conclude that answered prayers mean special favor, since stronger or braver people might be given harder tasks with less help.
standalone.insight: Receiving help may signal one's weakness rather than one's favor; the strong are given harder burdens.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Since refused prayers are often the lot of those who serve God best, ordinary believers should not take granted prayers as a sign of favor; it may reflect their weakness.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches the author's point.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: Fate as gods throwing dice, indifferent to what we would lose.
standalone.insight: Fate is indifferent to our wishes and attachments.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Fate, like the gods throwing dice, chooses us regardless of our plans or what we leave behind.
fidelity.reason: Consistent with the source; the later turn to love is simply omitted.

standalone.whatItIsAbout: The claim that sins of the flesh, though wrong, are the least serious kind of sin.
standalone.insight: Bodily sins are less grave than others, implying that the worst sins lie elsewhere.

fidelity.meaningInSource: Sins of the flesh are the least bad; the worst are spiritual ones like pride, power and hatred.
fidelity.reason: The standalone reading matches; the explanation of which sins are worse is omitted.
